title: EMC’s Wolf 620GE Is a 430-HP Old-School 4×4

body_markdown:
Whether it’s a product of Coventry or Graz, boxy, European off-roaders have a habit of evolving into ever more luxurious versions of their formerly utilitarian selves. Expedition Motor Company (EMC) has an offering that counters the proliferation of pillar-to-pillar touchscreens and total insulation from the outside world. We enjoyed one of the firm’s[diesel-powered Wolf models](https://www.hagerty.com/media/new-car-reviews/the-emc-wolf-g-wagen-is-a-bucket-of-restomod-fun/) a few years ago, so we looked forward to the chance to take a quick drive of the gasoline-powered 620GE to see how it would handle Monterey Car Week.


The two-door, open-top Wolf also comes with a fold-down windshield like a Wrangler, Scout, or Bronco.


[Brandan Gillogly](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/brandan-gillogly/)


EMC has been restoring and modifying Mercedes-Benz Geländewagens since 2017. Not just any of the boxy brutes, either. EMC exclusively revamps retired military 250GD models known by their “Wolf” nickname. For those of you who, like us, are a little rusty when it comes to Mercedes G-wagon nomenclature, that means the short-wheelbase, soft-top version of the W461 generation of solid-axle 4x4s built in the early ‘90s for military and first responders. The 250 denotes its 2.5-liter displacement, and GD is for Geländewagen Diesel.


Each EMC Wolf is stripped down to bare steel. More than 2500 man-hours go into every build.


Expedition Motor Company


I took a drive with Paul Stehn, Expedition Motor Company’s Product Director, who filled me in on this particular Wolf’s build and modification process. “Our production line is pretty standard,” explained Stehn. “We have two different lines. We have a short-wheelbase line, and a long-wheelbase line. Currently, short-wheelbase takes about six months; long-wheelbase takes an additional month on top of that.” Each donor vehicle is disassembled to its bare chassis before the steel body and chassis are stripped of all finishes. The chassis are powder-coated, and the bodies are given an anti-corrosion coating and then painted. Because the majority of the chassis and body are kept rather original, EMC can make plenty of progress before the customer makes their final decisions on paint, upholstery, and powertrain.


[Brandan Gillogly](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/brandan-gillogly/)


[Brandan Gillogly](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/brandan-gillogly/)

[Brandan Gillogly](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/brandan-gillogly/)


Each axle and transfer case gets a thorough rebuild. Double-cardan driveshafts reduce vibration.


Each EMC Wolf uses radius arm suspension front and rear, just like the original W461. It also keeps cable-actuated front and rear differential lockers, allowing all four tires to churn for traction over tough obstacles. While customers can select to have their Wolf powered by the original naturally aspirated inline-five diesel, there are several upgrades available. This Wolf is powered by a GM LS3 V-8 that produces more than 4.5 times the power of the original diesel. And that’s not because this is some monster-cammed, hot-rodded LS3—it’s just how the math works when comparing a 91-hp diesel to a mild-mannered LS3.


Expedition Motor Company


To ensure it has a steady supply of donor 250GDs in the wings, EMC has established contacts with militaries to get the first right of refusal when models are retired. The company builds 24 per year, split between two assembly lines.


Stehn noted that the integration of the LS3 focused on making it smooth, and the throttle response is gentle. “A lot of our clients buy them as family vehicles, so they don’t really want something that’s super high-strung.”


[Brandan Gillogly](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/brandan-gillogly/)


There are two basic built paths that customers choose. “There’s the period-correct, most authentic version: manual transmission with an OM 605 or OM 606 turbo-diesel,” Stehn explained, noting the Mercedes diesel has an agricultural clatter that some customers prefer, “and this is for someone who wants a bit more of a modern driver,” he said, referring to the China Blue Wolf we drove. While the naturally aspirated OM602 diesel offers the most affordable entry to the EMC Wolf, the LS3 powertrain in the model we drove represents the top of the line, and it’s priced as such. It’s a $20,000 premium on top of the optional 275-hp turbocharged OM606 version.


EMC offers suspension and brake upgrades to help handle the power and the modern highway speeds expected of the Wolf. This build uses adjustable Fox 2.0 reservoir shocks and G55 AMG brakes. Originally equipped with two-piston calipers up front and drums in the rear, the brakes were adequate for off-roading, but drums are known for fading fast.


[Brandan Gillogly](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/brandan-gillogly/)


Everything about the EMC Wolf feels rugged. The tailgate props open with a heavy metal latch; the doors take effort to close with a satisfying clunk. The details, however, were not ignored. The paint finish is phenomenal, the upholstery and trim are well fitted, and the center stack features upholstery with contrasting stitching. I noted that in the parking lot where we first drove the Wolf, it takes some effort to turn the large-diameter steering wheel. At highway speeds, it requires much less effort. Our drive on relatively smooth pavement only gave us a hint of the suspension’s on-road capability. Our initial impression was that the sway bars and shocks were a nice match, keeping things smooth and reducing body lean. Ample sidewalls also help soak up most minor pavement irregularities without transmitting shocks to the cabin.


EMC went through several iterations before it got a side-exit exhaust system that sounded right. The LS3’s exhaust uses an X-pipe and then loops around in a large-radius bend before making yet another 180 to route through mufflers and then exit in front of the rear tires. The system keeps the LS3 under wraps until about 4000rpm, when the V-8 comes alive at full throttle.


Expedition Motor Company


[Brandan Gillogly](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/brandan-gillogly/)

EMC integrated a double-DIN head unit to offer wireless Apple CarPlay and a backup camera. A Vintage Air HVAC control panel keeps things neat.


[Brandan Gillogly](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/brandan-gillogly/)


EMC’s restomodded Wolf seems to hit the sweet spot of classic and modern that so many enthusiasts are aiming for. The fuel-injected LS3 engine offers more than enough power, but there’s no auto start/stop, no cylinder deactivation, and the six-speed automatic offers a wide enough gear spread to keep the engine happy without constant shifting. Likewise, the interior is a mix of ‘90s Mercedes switchgear, but with smartly chosen modern upgrades. The Dakota Digital gauges, for example, offer analog sweep gauges for the speedometer, tachometer, fuel gauge, oil pressure, and coolant temperature while also offering a digital trip odometer and the option to more precisely monitor myriad engine parameters. As you’d expect for an upright vehicle with no top, exterior visibility is phenomenal.


As with any high-end restomod, the price of the EMC Wolf reflects the hours spent transforming a well-worn donor into an object of desire. The base Wolf, with its 2.5-liter naturally aspirated diesel engine, starts at $185,000. Add the LS3 with its 6L80 automatic, and the price climbs to more than $250,000. EMC has built more than 180 examples so far and has enough donors in stock to keep up with its plan of building 24 per year, proving that it’s found a niche in the analog 4×4 restomod market. After driving this one, it’s easy to see the appeal.
